routes.label: Coordinate components
Cosine laws in triangles with a derived cosine-difference step

changes.rationale: Let gamma=angle ACB. In triangle ABC, cos B=-3/5 and sin B=4/5 give AC^2=4^2+5^2-2*4*5*(-3/5)=65. The cosine law at C gives cos gamma=37/(5sqrt(65)); gamma is acute, so sin gamma=16/(5sqrt(65)). Since C is obtuse, cos C=-4/5. In the simple noncrossed configuration angle ACD=C-gamma. The explicitly printed h070 sine-difference identity and h064 cofunction reductions derive cos(C-gamma)=cos C cos gamma+sin C sin gamma=-4/sqrt(65). Applying the cosine law to ACD gives AD^2=65+400-40sqrt(65)*(-4/sqrt(65))=625, so AD=25. The old h071 special-value sum calculation is unnecessary; common support h063 supplies signed recovery from a known value/quadrant.

routes.label: Use the altitude and half-chord

changes.rationale: Let s=AB=BC and M be the midpoint of BC. O and A are on the perpendicular bisector of BC, and OA^2=48<R^2=156. Because O is outside the equilateral triangle it lies beyond A or beyond BC on this altitude line. The latter is impossible: OA=OM+AM would give OA^2>OM^2+AM^2=OM^2+3s^2/4>OM^2+s^2/4=R^2, contradicting OA<R. Thus O is beyond A. The retained altitude/Pythagorean route gives R^2=s^2/4+(4sqrt(3)+sqrt(3)*s/2)^2=s^2+12s+48. The additional law route has included angle OAB=150 degrees, so cos OAB=-sqrt(3)/2 and R^2=48+s^2-2*(4sqrt(3))*s*(-sqrt(3)/2)=s^2+12s+48. Both routes give (s-6)*(s+18)=0; the only positive side is s=6. routes.label: Derive a unique cyclic realization through a shared diagonal
Establish the unique cyclic realization with a shared diagonal and cosine laws

changes.rationale: For consecutive sides a,b,c,d, take shared diagonal t=BD with L=max(|a-d|,|b-c|)<t<U=min(a+d,b+c). The strict longest-side inequality ensures L<U. The cosine laws give cos A=(a^2+d^2-t^2)/(2ad) and cos C=(b^2+c^2-t^2)/(2bc). Their continuous sum is positive at the lower limiting endpoint and negative at the upper endpoint; it strictly decreases with t^2. Hence a unique t yields cos A+cos C=0. Since cosine is one-to-one on (0,pi), as derived by cofunction reduction and sine monotonicity, A+C=pi. Gluing the triangles on opposite sides of BD gives the unique convex cyclic realization for this ordered side tuple. Perimeter 32 permits exactly positive sides at most 15. There are C(31,3)-4*C(16,3)=2255 ordered tuples. Fifteen have period dividing two, of which (8,8,8,8) has period one. Counting rotation orbits, without identifying reflections, gives (2255-15)/4+(15-1)/2+1=568.

routes.label: Optimize using tangent lengths and half-angles
Bound the area by cosine laws and construct a tangential extremizer

changes.rationale: First consider a convex quadrilateral. If a disk of radius r fits inside it, splitting at the disk center gives K=(1/2)*sum(side_i*distance_i)>=21r. Put A,C for the opposite angles at sides (14,12) and (9,7). Applying the cosine law to the common diagonal gives 168 cos A-63 cos C=105. Right-triangle altitudes give 2K=168 sin A+63 sin C. The vector (105,2K)=168(cos A,sin A)+63(-cos C,sin C) has norm at most 231 by Cauchy-Schwarz and sin^2+cos^2=1. Therefore (2K)^2<=231^2-105^2=42336, so K<=42sqrt(6) and r<=2sqrt(6). Equality is constructible: use a radius sqrt(24) circle with successive vertex tangent lengths 8,6,3,4. Each positive half-angle is determined by its right-triangle ratio r/t. Opposite tangent-length products both equal r^2, so opposite half-angles are complementary; the four exterior turns sum to 2pi and define a convex tangent quadrilateral with sides 14,9,7,12. It is cyclic and attains both equalities. Concave quadrilaterals cannot improve the bound: their convex hull is a triangle. If the concave vertex is A,B or D, the hull retains two sides with shorter one 7,7 or 9, and triangle inradius < half that shorter side, at most 4.5<sqrt(24). If C is concave the hull has sides 12,14,t with 2<t<16. Put x=(26-t)/2, so 5<x<12. Heron and K=r*s give r_hull^2-24=[x^3-26x^2+192x-624]/(26-x). The numerator equals (x-16/3)^2*(x-46/3)-5072/27<0 throughout the interval. Thus no concave hull can hold a larger disk. The maximum is 2sqrt(6).

routes.label: Bound edges using Cartesian distances
Use polar-angle cosine laws to bound every polygon edge

changes.rationale: Factoring in z^4 gives (z^4-1)*(z^4+7+4sqrt(3)). The roots lie on radius 1 at angles k*pi/2 and on radius R=sqrt(2+sqrt(3)) at angles pi/4+k*pi/2. Inner-inner distances are at least sqrt(2), and outer-outer distances are at least R*sqrt(2). Between circles, the largest available cosine is cos(pi/4)=sqrt(2)/2, so squared cross-distance is at least 1+R^2-sqrt(2)*R=2, since sqrt(2)*R=1+sqrt(3). Thus every edge in any eligible 8-vertex polygon is at least sqrt(2). Alternating the eight roots in angular order gives a simple octagon all of whose sides equal sqrt(2), attaining perimeter 8sqrt(2).

routes.label: Angle-bisector ratios and Stewart's theorem

changes.rationale: Heron gives K=sqrt(39*12*13*14)=78sqrt(14), so r=K/39=2sqrt(14). The cosine law at B gives cos B=(27^2+25^2-26^2)/(2*27*25)=113/225.
